newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean by-election augurs well for ruling party.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean by-election augurs well for ruling party.

text.p: South Korean voters handed a thumping victory to the ruling party in a parliamentary by-election which analysts on Friday described as a warning to the opposition ahead of presidential polls.

Thursday's election in the central town of Yesan, a stronghold of opposition presidential candidate Kim Jong-pil, resulted in defeat for a candidate backed by the two opposition parties and was seen as a blow to the opposition's strategy of fielding a single candidate in December's presidential vote.
"The outcome is a blow to an opposition plan to cooperate in the presidential election," said the leading daily Dong-A Ilbo.

The Central Election Management Committee announced on Friday that candidate Oh Jang-sup of the ruling New Korea Party won a parliamentary seat with 26,608 votes against 23,312 for Cho Jong-souk of Kim Jong-pil's United Liberal Democrats.
To demonstrate the opposition's alliance, the largest opposition party, the National Congress for New Politics, did not field a candidate in Yesan and campaigned for Cho.
"This highlights the weakness of the two opposition parties' alliance against the ruling party," said Choi Jang-jip, political science professor at Korea University.

The two opposition parties have been negotiating in recent months to field a single candidate to improve their chances in December, although both Kim Jong-pil and Kim Dae-jung, National Congress leader, have been nominated as their torchbearers.
The Yesan poll was also the first chance for voters to pass judgment on the ruling party's choice on Monday of ex-supreme court judge Lee Hoi-chang as its presidential candidate.

Lee led the ruling party's campaign in Yesan, pointing out that he is from the central Chungchong province surrounding the town. Home-town loyalties and parochialism play decisive roles in South Korean elections.
"This is a turning point for Lee Hoi-chang to win in a stronghold for the Unitd Liberal Democrats," said Moon Chung-in, who lectures on politics at Yonsei University in Seoul.
"The ruling party's victory shows Lee now has the support of the region," he said.
Cho had won in the same constituency in general elections last year but the election committee ordered a fresh poll after his campaign manager was jailed for election law violations.
In another by-election on Thursday, independent Park Tae-joon, a former ruling party elder, won the vacant National Assembly seat representing the industrial town of Pohang.
The victory for Park, who quit the ruling party over policy differences with President Kim Young-sam, was widely expected, but it again underscored the weakness of the opposition.

Park ran against Lee Ki-taek, a former leader of the main opposition who now heads a splinter grouping, the Democratic Party. Park captured 77,884 votes against Lee's 35,137, while political novice Lee Byung-suk, who ran for the ruling party, got 17,801 votes.
Political analysts noted that no opposition party candidate has ever won a presidential race.
Yonsei University's Moon said the Yesan vote illustrated the opposition's feebleness and that it was probably doomed to lose in December even if it managed to forge a united front.

Lee, who built a reputation as "Mr Clean" while serving as a judge, was earlier this year asked by President Kim to lead the beleaguered New Korea Party, which has been rocked by a string of corruption scandals.
